utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is the 21st of July, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Scott and his associates, and to all the people helping us. First of all, I shall give the floor to the registrar for a few IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Buntic, Zoran. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00827. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00828. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00829. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00830. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00831. And finally, the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number 00832. Thank you. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You wanted the floor, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, ever so briefly. Can we go into private session for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D is about to cross-examine. You have 2 hours and 60 seconds. As you see, it's very exact indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. You know that the cross-examination is going to resume. Ms. Alaburic is the one among the Defence counsel who is going to cross-examine you first. She is to be followed by the Prosecutor for his own cross-examination. You may proceed. Oh, yes. Ms. Alaburic, my fellow Judge reminds me of this. If you are to tackle new topics, you have to say so, and if you ask questions that arise from the examination-in-chief, then it will be credited as part of your cross-examination. If you tackle a new topic, you have to say that ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Zuzul. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honour, I believe that all of my questions will in a certain way be related to documents and topics that have been raised or shown during direct examination, but if you still feel that I'm going beyond the scope of direct examination, I will not be opposed to you treating that time as the time allocated to the Defence of General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zuzul, I believe you remember where we left off, and I will continue according to the plan that I had made already in May. Let me remind you of one question asked by His Honour Judge Antonetti relating to documents of the United Nations. You were asked if you could point out Resolution, a report of the Secretary-General containing major errors. The question and answer are on 27713 page of the transcript, and the next page, 27714. You answered, Mr. Zuzul, that you had not observed any major errors, but what you could hold against perhaps the international community was their attempt to balance out the responsibilities. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What kind of balancing out of responsibilities were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In more than one meeting that I personally had with representatives of the international community I heard the response that neither in Croatia, in UNPROFOR protected areas, or in Bosnia-Herzegovina were they there to establish responsibility or to apportion blame. They were there just to observe what was happening on the ground without taking into account the broader picture, and that created the impression that there was an attempt to artificially balance out the responsibilities, because if you take into account that that part of the territory of Croatia had been occupied before the UNPROFOR came, and when you are trying to report only as of a certain moment without taking into account what had happened before, the resulting picture is objectively inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, tell me, were you relatively well informed about the developments in Croatia in those years, in the '90s, in order to be able to assess whether a certain UN report does or does not contain errors?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was relatively well informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you equally well informed of developments and events in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about events on the ground in Bosnia and Herzegovina, of course I was not as well informed as of happenings in Croatia, but I knew the overall situation and especially the course of negotiations on the former Yugoslavia. I was relatively well informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic that concerns the transcript that you discussed on the 7th of May with the Defence of Prlic, P 00131. It's in the binder of Prlic Defence. I have to admit I don't know which number of the binder because there were several. I believe that you don't even need to see the document. I'll try to remind you of certain portions of that transcript and then we could go through them together. It's a transcript from a meeting between President Tudjman and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, the staff of the Croatian army, and the military commanders held on the 4th of March, 1992, and in direct examination you spoke about it in the context of the defence of southern Croatia. In that meeting you were represented [as interpreted], Mr. Zuzul, as a psychologist in the IPD administration of the Republic of Croatia. Was that really the case in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of March 1992 that was my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. This reads in the transcript you were represented as a psychologist. Did you mean you were presented as a psychologist? The sentence does not really make sense, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to say that he was introduced as a psychologist. So everybody when starting to speak gave their background first, and that's how Mr. Zuzul had introduced himself, as a psychologist at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This document is already exhibited in the case, and I believe it contains some important positions that I would like you to explain, Mr. Zuzul, as a participant in that discussion. At that meeting, it's on page 46 of the English transcript, you pointed out the existence of two categories of people. One category, former members of the Yugoslav People's Army; and the second category, those who had never been in that army. And then you tried to point out that in certain segments of the Republic of Croatia there was a certain tension between those two categories of people. Do you remember giving that caution?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know at this moment is the view of President Tudjman. Tell us, did President Tudjman believe that anyone who wanted to commit themselves to defence of the country, regardless of whether they had previously been officers of the JNA, should be able to find their place either in the army or in some other part of the war effort?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I can testify from direct knowledge and direct communication with President Tudjman that he indeed believed that, because only two days after this contribution to the discussion I made President Tudjman invited me for a talk. We discussed precisely this subject and even -- and he even offered me a position in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you help us understand another statement made by late President Tudjman. On page 92 of the English transcript he said and I will quote: "As I believe Professor Zuzul mentioned do not make any political statements. And generally speaking, the army has no place in the political arena." Tell us, Mr. Zuzul, did President Tudjman really believe that the army should concern themselves with the defence of the country rather than being a political factor?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion at the time was that President Tudjman held the view that for the defence of the country and for the purposes of creating an army it would be best if the army stayed out of politics as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Another very important statement, in fact a three-page speech in the English transcript, that's 103 through 105, I'll try to remind you. On this occasion late President Tudjman said that the US has still not recognised Croatia, and there were some politicians in the US who still viewed Croatia in a way as a continuation of the Independent State of Croatia from the time of World War II, and he reminded us that certain factors, certain players like the HOS were still taking pictures with the symbol "U" and the iconography of the independent State of Croatia, and Tudjman said, I quote, "They are fascists. They are a continuation of the independent State of Croatia." And he called upon all the commanders of the Croatian army to firmly oppose that and to prevent any attempt of any soldier to identify himself with any ideology that is similar or identical to Fascist ideologies of World War II. Do you think that Tudjman really supported a Fascist policy of that previous state, the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all my discussions with late President Tudjman, I only heard anti-Fascist views from him. Generally speaking, it is well known that late President Tudjman was an active fighter against Fascism, and to add a personal note, it was indeed a subject that I discussed with him quite often because my father had also been actively involved in the struggle against Fascism. Not in Croatia or in Yugoslavia but in Belgium. So we discussed it quite often. I was a young man then, and I was quite interested in hearing his views and his thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, President Tudjman was Tito's general, as the phrase went.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zuzul, I'd appreciate it if you could try to comment on certain statements and events related to Vance-Owen's Peace Plan and the events in January 1993. You were familiar with the negotiations, and you knew about the plans of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 1st of February, 1993, that's true. I became the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia to Geneva, and among other things my job was to monitor the peace talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the course of those talks did you come to know Mr. Herbert Okun?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will put to you some of his statements, and you will tell me whether they are correct, accurate, or not. So one statement goes like this: "Croats were full of enthusiasm, not only about maps but the whole Vance-Owen Plan." It's on transcript page 16752. Tell us, Dr. Zuzul, this evaluation about the enthusiasm of Croats, is that accurate in your view or not?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he noted it accurately. I don't know if I, myself, would use the term "enthusiasm," but I would say that the Croats, generally speaking, readily accepted the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the next page of the transcript Mr. Herbert Okun said: "The Bosnian Croats signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in January 1993 knowing that Serbs, and to a lesser extent Muslims, would not accept the package." To the best your knowledge did Croats really accept the Vance-Owen Plan sincerely and completely, or they were reckoning that the other side would not go through with it and it will be dead in the water anyway, that it was just pure calculation on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's much easier for me to talk about the positions, the official positions, of Croatia. I can say that official Croatia truly and with all seriousness accepted the Vance-Owen Plan, because we believed it was conducive to a solution in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also to a solution to the problems in Croatia, because part of Croatia had been occupied still, and to a general diffusion of tensions. As for my colleagues from Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had occasion to talk with many of them at that time, although I did not represent them officially, and it was my impression that they, too, were embracing the plan sincerely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you now give us your comments on certain observations made by Mr. Okun regarding maps? Mr. Okun told us the discussions on maps were continuous and marked by dispute, constant dispute. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In my set of documents, I prepared P 9276. Those are maps. Among others, maps of Banovina Croatia and certain provinces in Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the Vance-Owen Plan from January 1993. The document has been exhibited. Could you please open the documents marked "Banovina '39," and another document, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, 2nd January 1993. We will not go into detail. Instead, I'd like to look at conclusions that can be made at first blush. If we look at these maps, Mr. Zuzul, can we agree that the territory designated as part of the Banovina of 1939 in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina is very similar to what the Croatian provinces used to be in the Vance-Owen Plan of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's right. It's rather similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in addition to these two maps, did you see any other maps during the negotiations which had marked as Croatian territory areas smaller or larger than these?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the negotiations numerous maps were shown. The territory varied. It was on occasion larger, on occasion smaller than the one we have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we tried to identify a common denominator of all these maps, would we assert that all these maps had marked as Croatian territory Western Herzegovina, that is the area around Tomislavgrad, Posusje, Grude, Ljubuski, and so on. Around Tomislavgrad, Posusje, Ljubuski, Grude, and so on. Let me not go into all the municipalities involved. Then an area of Central Bosnia and a part of the Bosnian Posavina. In other words, these three groups of territories or areas. Can we agree on that, Mr. Zuzul?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we were to try to look at the ethnicity criterion and the economic units and so on and so forth and try and identify the areas where the Croats were in an absolute or relative majority, and if we came up with a territory which made a more or less sensible area, would that territory again include Western Herzegovina, parts of Central Bosnia, and Bosnian Posavina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt counsel, but I am just concerned for the accuracy of the record and so that we all know what we're talking about here. I can appreciate that counsel doesn't want to necessarily go through all of the municipalities claimed to comprise Herceg-Bosna, but there might in fact, and the Prosecution in fact would take the position that there's another category of territory that is neither Western Herzegovina nor Central Bosnia. In looking at the map, if the Chamber has that available, the Prosecution might agree in fact that when one uses the terminology "Western Herzegovina," that might indeed be the so-called border municipalities of Livno, Tomislavgrad, Posusje, Grude, Ljubuski. We would not agree that Western Herzegovina, for example, includes Jablanica, nor do we think Jablanica is part of Central Bosnia. So therefore when certain questions are put to Mr. Zuzul which do not -- do not fully set out the territory described, there is substantial area for confusion or lack of clarity. So counsel might -- if she insists or wants to know this material accurately, she may have to get a bit more detail, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank my learned friend Mr. Scott on the comment. I must say that I'm not quite clear with the gist of his objection. Let me just draw your attention that my question to Mr. Zuzul did not relate to the area of Central Bosnia. I spoke of the territories marked as Banovina in 1939 and the territories marked as the Croatian provinces under the Vance-Owen Plan of January 1993. In other words, I did not mention Herceg-Bosna in any way, so that his remarks relating to Jablanica and other areas is -- are quite unfounded, and it's not my intention to discuss the area of Herceg-Bosna with Mr. Zuzul. I clearly expressed what I wanted to discuss about in my question. I'm sure the witness answered the question -- or, rather, by looking at the transcript, I can see that the witness did not in fact answer my question, and I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to request the witness to answer the question. Let us forget for a moment that Herceg-Bosna ever existed. If anyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to set up a third entity, the so-called Croat entity based on economic criteria or the criteria of it being an economic and regional entity and ethnic entity, would that individual come up with a territory that includes Western Herzegovina, parts of Central Bosnia, and parts of Bosnian Posavina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can testify to is that based on my knowledge of the work of the work group and the negotiating party is that they drew their maps precisely based on the criteria you mentioned, namely, ethnic, economic, and spatial or territorial criteria. At any rate, it was experts from the international community who drew these maps rather than the local players from the area, although I believe that the latter would have come up with more or less the same maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zuzul, can you now comment upon the possibility of defining the States which arose from the former Yugoslavia. In your binder you have document 4D 540. This document has been exhibited, and this is the opinion of the Badinter Commission defining the conditions based on which the republics of the former Yugoslavia could be recognised as states. There is no need to read that. You'll remember that. One of the criteria set out the following: That the republics of the former Yugoslavia would be recognised in what were then their republican borders. First of all, Mr. Zuzul, were you aware of this view held by the Badinter Commission?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the Badinter Commission advanced their conclusions before I became actively involved in diplomatic work, I was fully aware as a private citizen, and later on as a diplomat, of what they were about. And if I can say, the vast majority of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia gladly accepted such a decision. After all these years, I can only repeat that this was the only proper decision, that is that the borders of the new states could only be defined as the borders of the then republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, 4D 00542. This is a document of the Council of Ministers of the European Community, guidelines for the recognition of the new states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. The document dates from December 1991. The last bullet on page 1 says: "Acknowledging the inviolability of all borders that can be changed only through peaceful means and joint agreement." Mr. Zuzul are you aware of this document issued by the Council of Ministers of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this document. It was on the basis of this document that Slovenia and Croatia were recognised roughly a month later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was it a fact that the professional expert public at large supported the idea that the new states arising from the former Yugoslavia should have as borders the so-called AVNOJ borders?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. Let me just say something that goes beyond the scope of your question, but I was reminded of that by these documents. On several occasions in the course of that process, in the course of this trial, and I saw this in the indictment as well, that there was a wish for Croatia to be defined within the borders of Banovina Hrvatska, of the Croatian Banovina. The document we have now on our screens proves the absurdity of such a premise or such an aspiration. The Croatian Banovina did not include important parts of the Republic of Croatia; namely, Istria, one of the most significant and most beautiful parts of Croatia; the town of Rijeka with over 200.000 inhabitants; the town of Zadar with almost 100.000 inhabitants. In other words, if someone offered the citizens of Croatia the borders of the Croatian Banovina whereby they would lose the territory where, roughly speaking, half a million of inhabitants live at present, territory which is at any case an integral part of the Republic of Croatia, in exchange for something that cannot in any way, either historically or territorially, be compared, I don't believe that such an individual offering something like that would be taken in earnest. Truth to tell, I am not aware of or I don't know a single serious individual who, if offered the map of the Croatian Banovina and the map of the current Republic of Croatia, who would in all common sense vote for the former.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your extensive answer, but you left out Baranja which was also not part of the Croatian Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's also look at another document which also has to do with the same topic. This is 34428 [as interpreted]. It's also been exhibited. This is an Official Note from the meeting with the -- with the French delegation. This was compiled by General Anton Tus. Please turn to page 2. Let me repeat the number of the document. 3D, so it's the document of the Defence for General Praljak, 3D 00482. Now we have the correct number. At page 2 -- the document dates from January 1993, and the meeting took place on the 13th of January. At page 2 of the document, the words uttered by General Praljak are conveyed. Let me quote that. "The Croats are committed to an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the rights of Croats. The problems between Muslims and Croats in the BH are the result of different objectives of the political struggles. Croats are fighting for state of the BH with an autonomy for Croats whereas the Muslims are struggling for a civic state. So it follows clearly from this that the Croats are also struggling for state of the BH." Let's look at page 3, the end of the penultimate paragraph where General Tus spoke. The Geneva conference offers a solution for the BH on equal footing. The creation of a Serb state in the BH would be an error that would not contribute to the resolution of the Serbian issue in the Republic of Croatia. In connection with this document and in particular in relation to the view or the premise expressed by General Tus, let me put the following questions to you, Dr. Zuzul, as an individual who was on quite close terms with President Tudjman, and you can base your testimony on first-hand knowledge. Did the Republic of Croatia in the AVNOJ borders represent a certain value which President Tudjman would not jeopardise under any circumstances, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly, yes. That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was President Tudjman aware of the possibility that by separating parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and forming and independent state would call into question the very survival of the AVNOJ republican borders as well as the issue of the survival of the Republic of Croatia in the AVNOJ borders? In other words, would such a development in Bosnia-Herzegovina also legitimise the right of the Serb people in the Republic of Croatia to ask for the -- for the one-third of the territory that was under their occupation to be separated, to secede?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was aware of that, and such a danger most definitely existed. I will not go into a discussion about how far such a view, if held by the Croatian Serbs, would have been legitimate. However, the fact of the matter is that back in 1993 or 1994, the Serbs in the so-called Krajina in Croatia and the Serbs from the so-called Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina had made formal decisions on the issue, that is, to get united. This would most definitely place the borders and even the very existence of the republic of Croatia in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zuzul, in your opinion did late President Tudjman consider the position of the international community serious, its position that it would not allow for the borders of the republics of the former Yugoslavia to be changed by force?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that he regarded it as serious and that he was convinced that forcible change of borders would not be allowed. However, oftentimes during international negotiations there was mention of the possibility to change borders through peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you now clarify what you've just said, the fact that the negotiations mentioned the change of borders through peaceful means? Which particular borders of the Republic of Croatia are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only example I'm aware of where President Tudjman accepted to engage in such talks was the possibility of swapping the territories in the area of Neum in Bosnia-Herzegovina for certain parts of territories in Croatia. This is something I spoke of earlier on. Proposals for territories to be swapped was something that we were -- we received on several occasions. For instance, I heard repeatedly that Croatia would not be in a position to reintegrate Eastern Slavonia and that we should best negotiate with the Republic of Serbia in order to have this territory exchanged for -- or swapped either for the territory of the Bosnian Posavina, and I heard indirectly on two occasions the Serb side proposing that that particular territory be swapped for the occupied territory around Knin. In other words, we were supposed to swap a piece of Croatian territory for another piece of Croatian territory. In a nutshell, not once did I observe President Tudjman agreeing to such talks to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, can you now clarify the statement that you made about the -- the part of the territory around Neum? Were these negotiations which were supposed to result in the possibility for Bosnia-Herzegovina to have a proper harbour for its economic purposes on the Croatian coast?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is Muslim representatives, always emphasised the issue of access to the sea as one of the key issues in all negotiations, and then the issue of Neum and the status of Neum arose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Zuzul, as opposed to these statements about realpolitik and the standpoints of the international community, I would like to confront you with some statements of President Tudjman about the borders of Republic of Croatia that he sometimes called absurd. Sometimes he called them unnatural. Sometimes he said that Croatia is the only state in the world that looks like a croissant, that it's simply not natural to begin with. Let me ask you, this statement of late President Tudjman about the unnaturalness and absurdity of Croatian borders, were they reflected in the press? Could people read about it in newspapers, hear it on television?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we, on the contrary, then infer that nobody learned of these views of Mr. Tudjman by wiretapping or any other spy means of gathering intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. As far as I remember, President Tudjman made such a statement in one public debate after the first free and democratic elections in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean the one about the croissant.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, late President Tudjman was an historian?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As a high official in Croatian politics and a collaborator of President Tudjman, have you ever noticed that those statements were part of the official views of President Tudjman and official positions of the Croatian policy and that they affected the foreign policy of Croatia and the state policy in general?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me some time, I will tell you about my impressions. It always seemed to me that President Tudjman approached certain problems in two ways. First of all as an historian who had spent decades of his life studying the situation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, inter-ethnic relations in that region. And as an historian and as a philosopher, I would say that he liked to think in terms of theories of major international solutions. When he spoke from that point of view wearing his historian hat, Dr. Tudjman would expound on all the problems that attended the creation of Bosnia and the problems related to Bosnia and Herzegovina in both the first and the second Yugoslavia, and he did express doubts about the viability of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the future. At any rate, he's not the only historian or philosopher or politician who held or expressed those views. We can still hear them nowadays. However, as a statesman who in his own words had an historic opportunity to create a sovereign State of Croatia, I believe that he acted rationally and pragmatically, and he accepted the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina has been internationally recognised and accepted as a state. And from the entirety of his conduct as a head of state, I would say that his activities, if you want me to say directly, and I know that from instructions he gave to us diplomats and others, I believe, too, his activities were directed at preserving Bosnia and Herzegovina, but while protecting Croats inside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional explanation, Dr. Zuzul. When you attended these international talks, did you observe certain participants in the talks, not only as one of the participants yourself, as a politician, but also a psychologist?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am a psychologist by training. I've spent a good part of my life working as a professor of psychology, and I believe that I could use the same analogy as most of you esteemed lawyers are unable to look at a document without assessing its legal aspects. Similarly, for most of us psychologists, it's hard to abstract our training. But at the same time I'm not saying that my conclusions as a psychologist are more accurate than any conclusions a layman could make.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you some documents, and I'll ask you to comment looking at these documents. The approach of the delegation led by President Alija Izetbegovic, as representatives of one of the three warring sides of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe the documents will help us understand better. The first document is 4D 01118. It's a transcript from the session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 26th November 1993. I'll ask you, Mr. Zuzul, about something on page 4 in B/C/S. In English it's page marked DD003364. One of the topics here is demilitarisation. To the best of your recollection was demilitarisation one of the topics discussed at international talks?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here and there the issue would crop up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at what Alija Izetbegovic said about the position of his delegation. I quote: "I would say a couple of words about demilitarisation. Another position has to be defended. When we accepted this demilitarisation, we reckoned this way. Light infantry weapons won't be surrendered by anyone certainly, so who will be demilitarised? Those who have heavy weapons will be demilitarised. Therefore, it won't affect us. That was our reasoning. Certain forms of demilitarisation do not affect us, because they will have to surrender tanks and turn over heavy artillery over to be supervised. They would surrender 100 tanks, whereas we would surrender 4 to 10. I don't know what the ratio is currently. In artillery the ratio is 1 to 10, whereas everyone will hide light weaponry, of course, or they will hand it over to the police. So we thought there could be a way of removing those tanks from Bosnia. However, after touring Bosnia and Herzegovina, it seems to us that we need the army too. We need an army too. And we need to ensure," I am sorry about the way these sentences sound, but I'm just reading. "This army has to exist as an army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Demilitarisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina does not really suit us because no one would be protecting us then." Dr. Zuzul, to the best of your knowledge did the Muslim delegation really support demilitarisation for a while and then after a certain point they stopped supporting that principle because they decided it would be contrary to their interests? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally think that demilitarisation had never been taken seriously by anyone. No one ever considered it a serious option, because I believe the Serbian side or the Yugoslav army was not prepared to hand over their weapons. And it was equally clear that the international community had no resolve, did not have the required resolve to take the weaponry away from them. It is quite certain that for Croatia, and especially for the Muslim side in the beginning of the war this demilitarisation would have been useful and good. But as I said, nobody ever believed it possible. However, if you allow me to say this as a psychologist, to venture a comment, I knew and held in high esteem Mr. Alija Izetbegovic as a man who was visibly deeply concerned for the fate of his people, but I believe this passage that you've just read was quite typical of his approach to negotiations. In this very brief passage, he advocates two completely opposite stands. In the first few sentences he supports demilitarisation, and in the next couple of sentences he's against it. And that's when he was addressing his own parliament, if I'm not mistaken. That frequently happened at the negotiations, even in direct negotiations and talks. And if I may say one more thing, it appeared to me that it sometimes led to problems in communication between him and President Tudjman. As a rule, President Tudjman was the kind of person who, when he made a decision, and he was relatively firm when he made decisions, he was keen on seeing it through. President Izetbegovic, on the other hand, and I have to emphasise I'm speaking from my own personal experience, had difficulty in making decisions. And even when he made a decision, it was not yet certain that he would really carry it out. By this I don't mean to say anything bad about him, but I believe that I'm not alone in thinking like this. There are many other people who had occasion to observe him and who think the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I thought we would come to that when we see some more passages from this transcript, but I believe what you just said is going to be confirmed by what follows. Let us look at the next passage. In Croatian it's on page 13 onwards, and in English it's DD003374 onwards. I'll quote it here. "Alija Izetbegovic says that only US supports integral Bosnia," and he says, I'm saying this for the benefit of Judge Antonetti, "all this is for nothing when Mitterrand is leading the policy in France."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please start reading again and tell us where she's reading from, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me repeat part of my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After a brief comment, "What's the use from France when it's led by Mitterrand?" Then Tudjman says: "The objective of the policy is to fight for an integral Bosnia," and then I quote: "I don't see at this moment any forces that could carry this idea through. I don't see any. Just point your finger. What are those forces that could carry the idea of an integrated Bosnia through? If you mean the army, the army can defend these people here and these areas here, and by exerting its pressure, with some additional pressure from us through politics, we could broaden that area perhaps a little bit, but the army is not strong enough to go all the way to Banja Luka. It's futile even to talk about it. Only idealists with no sense of reality can talk about that." I'll end the quotation here. Tell me, Dr. Zuzul, Banja Luka was the capital of Republika Srpska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the two capitals in the view of the Bosnian Serbs. One was Banja Luka and the other Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, as a person who relatively -- knew the situation there relatively well, did Izetbegovic want to say that the BH army did not have the strength to reach Banja Luka or to liberate the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that your interpretation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Zuzul, based on your participation in international conferences, was it clear that the -- the Muslim delegation led by Alija Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I refer to your question before, which I understood to be a question of whether one or the other, and the answer is, "I believe your interpretation is correct." So the answer is it's either or the other, but probably you were asking for an answer as to which it was, one or the other, and that cannot be answered by "yes" very well. This is an exception to the rule that you must answer "yes," "no," "I can't say." It may again be a linguistic problem. I'm referring to page 26, lines 6 to 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me clarify these -- the word "or," which referred to the following: To arrive -- to reach Banja Luka or to liberate the territory depending on how you interpret it. This would be an aggression in view of the Serbs, and now for Croats and Muslims this would mean liberation. So my question was not placed this as opposed to the other but meaning -- liberation meaning the BH army reaching Banja Luka. I believe that Dr. Zuzul understood my question properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, he said -- he did not have a translation either, so it's easier for him, but I thank you for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zuzul, I had a feeling you were about to add something. If not, we can move on to the next question. To your knowledge, based on your participation in international conferences, was it clear that the Bosniak Muslim delegation was in favour of a united Bosnia-Herzegovina as opposed to the state model of a federation, confederation, or anything else of the sort?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To qualify the conduct of the Bosnian Muslim delegation unequivocally, I believe that they espoused the idea of a united Bosnia-Herzegovina as a unitarian state and more so in the political than in the territorial sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. Let us look at the page 19 of the Croatian text and page 3380 of the English version. We have a very short conclusion by Alija Izetbegovic which I will read fully. I quote: "We can make one conclusion so far. The delegation should go up there. More or less we know what the platform is, plus those efforts regarding the extension of functions and territories, plus the failure to sign and so on and so forth. Can we go there with such instructions? Let's see and come back." Dr. Zuzul, based on this it is quite clear that the Bosnia delegation received an instruction here not to sign documents whatsoever, to attend the event but to come back without having signed anything. Based on your experience, were there situations where the Bosnian delegation indeed comported this way?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never had occasion to see an address by Mr. Izetbegovic to his delegation in such clear terms. However, my impression on many occasions had been that they did not have the intention to arrive at a solution but that they negotiated for the sake of negotiating or for the sake of buying time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see how the positions of the Bosniak delegations evolved. Now let us look at 4D 01052. 01052. This is the transcript from the Presidency session of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 29th of December, 1993. I selected the portions I felt were the most important. One of them, maybe not so important but equally interesting, can be found at page -- we're following the enumeration in the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I may again have misunderstood something, but we have a title with the number, and that speaks of a meeting of the 29th of December, but then we have the transcript itself which speaks of 26th of December, and I'd be grateful if you told me what I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can you just tell me where it is that the 26th of December is written since I don't have that date in my document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's the opening page. It's the very first page. In the English translation, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. It's a translation error. So this is an error in the English translation. It is indeed the 233rd session, but as you can see in the original version, the date is the 29th. I apologise for not checking whether the two tally. I did not look at all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zuzul, this is what I wanted you to comment upon. Let us look at the enumeration in our language. It's in the lower right-hand corner. Look at the enumeration, 0700. In English that's at pages 26 and 27. I will tell you briefly what the BH Presidency discussed here. They said that it was inappropriate for Boban's army to be called Ustasha, because according to an investigation conducted by the Globus, Globus weekly, because they had the -- Boban's troops had 221 years' membership in the party, and they are not Fascists. They should not be called Highwaymen, Vampires and such like. So they should not be called Vampires, Boban's Men, so on and so forth. In your opinion, Dr. Zuzul, how did the Bosnian leadership -- the Bosnian Muslim leadership refer to the leadership of Herceg-Bosnia? How did they style them or call them? Do you have any knowledge to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not really want to go into what they called them officially, but it is true that the media did use that particular term dating from World War II, the terms harking back to the Ustasha and Chetniks. This particular term could not have been used by Croats and Muslims given the events of World War II since both -- there were both Croats and Muslims who were members of either the Partisans, on the one hand, or the Ustasha on the other. This is street slang, not to say the slang of the underworld which found its way to the public at large through the media. I was not aware of such terminology ever having been used at official meetings such as this one, but I was always aware of the fact that this made communication more difficult. And I mean communication in general between peoples and politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at what Alija Izetbegovic said at page 703 onwards. That's at page 29 of the English version, 29 onwards. That's the very end of December 1993. The BH army launched an offensive in Central Bosnia. We will be coming to that part of the transcript later on. What we are interested in at the moment is the following, and I quote: "When it comes to the specific conduct of the army in Central Bosnia, what they say on the issue of negotiations, it literally says: Nothing has been agreed upon until everything has been agreed upon. Therefore, Central Bosnia -- a deal was not reached on Central Bosnia. Armija still has a free-hand in -- in terms of conducting actions since no deal has yet been made." Dr. Zuzul, to your knowledge was it the policy of the Bosnia delegation always such that one issue would be left open, would not be agreed upon, so that pursuant to this particular policy, according to which nothing has been agreed upon until everything has been agreed upon, new -- or, rather, all issues would be raised for discussion again, issues that were considered settled by other parties to the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with any certainty whether the Muslim Bosniak side acted deliberately in that respect. However, on several occasions and at several negotiations I observed not only Mr. Izetbegovic but other representatives of the Muslims expressing the view that nothing had been agreed upon until everything was agreed upon. I specifically remember one occasion where during an interval in the negotiations, as an individual who had by that time been studying the theory of negotiations and where more -- speaking more as -- as an intellectual then than a politician, I -- I tried to reason with them that complex political relations could not be addressed or resolved through -- through such a position. I tried to reason with them on several occasions, but they insisted on taking that course and thus continued in their resolve to leave these negotiations open without any specific solutions. On the other hand, international negotiators were rather inclined to accept such negotiating position because it made it easier for them to hold these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With your permission. Mr. Zuzul, in your view is this a wrong attitude? Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, or is it a possible attitude in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a position that was possible and oftentimes expressed. However, in most negotiations that are of a complex nature, and these particular negotiations were of a very complex nature, such a position, and I believe I -- many experts would agree with me on this, such a position leads to an impasse. For instance, in order for them to be able to agree upon political solutions a truce has to be introduced first. If you say that a truce cannot be introduced because political settlements have not been made, you -- you obstruct negotiations. I have now remembered that this was what they specifically did. Whenever we said that he would should find a framework solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, they would say, "Well, yes, but we did not really agree upon how individual municipality would be -- municipalities would be divided amongst us." So the global solution could not be reached because not everything has been agreed upon. However, if you look at the principles of negotiations, you cannot even go into resolving details unless you have found a framework solution. That was my opinion at the time, and that is still my opinion. I cannot claim that the Muslim side did this to deliberately obstruct negotiations, or as I described it on several occasions, to buy time. It was my impression that the Muslim side, particularly Mr. Izetbegovic, were convinced that their negotiating position would strengthen over time. However, I repeat that was only an impression on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time for the break now. We're going to break for 20 minutes. I inform the Petkovic Defence that it still has 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I believe that Judge Prandler has a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic, to take your time, but just one minute. It is, of course, not your time, but ours. So I would simply would like to confirm, as far as my position is concerned, that I would have asked the same question from Mr. Zuzul like what has been asked by Judge Trechsel, and also in view of the -- my experience in the given field, that is the international negotiations, I believe that that very principle which was mentioned has been -- in general has been adopted as a positive one. So that is why without losing too much time I would only like to -- to ask Mr. Zuzul, Dr. Zuzul, if you really feel that the given principle has prevented you, I mean the Croatian side, to proceed with the negotiations and to reach some positive results. It is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, by no means did it prevent the Croatian side. The Croatian side never even thought or said that it could thwart us. I was speaking of the position of the Muslim side by saying that when you have long-lasting negotiations, you have been negotiating for days and then you reach a point of agreement, if any of the sides holds on to the principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, and if they interpret that principle as meaning that everything that had been agreed previously is null and void, then that could practically thwart, disable the negotiations. That's how I interpreted that principle. It wasn't always the case, but sometimes I had the impression that that's the way the Muslim side interpreted this principle itself. Let me illustrate again. We had been negotiating for two days or five days or ten days, but if one side adheres to the principle that none of these agreements are worth anything unless we agree on the minutest detail on the 14th day, and if they proceed from that principle, then on day 13 we will reach a point when they say none of our agreements hold true. We have to start again. And as I've said already, if you accept this principle in theory and in practice, then it makes it impossible to reach an agreement. And my impression was that sometimes, not always but sometimes, that's the way negotiations were led. I hope, Your Honour, I manage to clarify what I really meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Zuzul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you may proceed. I was a little too generous earlier on. I told you 45 minutes, but it's actually 43 minutes according to our calculations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for this generosity. I hope I will return it with even greater generosity by not using up all of the 43 minutes. I thank the Judges for these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zuzul, can we try to boil this down to two main standpoints? Can we agree that unless all elements of one agreement are agreed then this agreement has not been reached?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if one delegation in these negotiations deliberately and consciously conducts the negotiations in such a way as to always leave one element not agreed on the principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, that can make the negotiations endless. And can we then say that it is a way of obstructing the negotiations by making agreement impossible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I wonder whether it's quite correct to again speak of deliberate, whereafter the witness has said that he could not affirm that there was a deliberate policy behind that. I think this is not entirely correct. Perhaps you want to reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question now is phrased very generally, and it doesn't concern the specific policy of the Muslim delegation now. It's a general question. It can apply in other situations to Croats. I am not trying to examine this principle on the factual level. We're going to do that with other witnesses, and we have numerous documents about it even now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in principle, Mr. Zuzul, regardless of who it concerns, if one delegation behaves in the way I described, if they always leave one issue open, can that be considered as an obstruction of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that it can, and in my answer to His Honour Judge Prandler, I tried to illustrate why I believe it can indeed be obstruction. If one legitimate principle is taken as absolute, namely, the principle nothing is agreed until everything is, then this principle is used to destroy the entire process. Negotiations are only negotiations if all the sides are talking bona fide in the desire to reach an agreement; otherwise, it's obstruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zuzul. Let us look at the transcript again. We were talking about attacks on Vitez. On page in Croatian 704 and English page 29, Stjepan Kljuic is trying to raise the issue wouldn't it be a good idea if the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina moved to liberate Foca rather than moving at Vitez, and he goes on to say that from the standpoint of Bosnia and Herzegovina and from the viewpoint of the Muslim people, "Foca would be more important to us." Dr. Zuzul, tell us, which side held the territory of Foca under its control?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who held Foca at that moment, but judging by what is said here -- in fact, I'd rather not interpret what Mr. Kljuic meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Several pages later, Croatian 709, English 33 and 34, Mr. Siber, who was deputy commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he says this analysis is interesting -- I'm quoting from 710, the end of his contribution. I quote: "I'm telling you that the BH army has the strength with regard to Busovaca, Vitez, and the part of Novi Travnik currently held by HVO under the absolute control of Boban's men and the Herzegovina men, save for Kiseljak where the UNPROFOR is located and when -- where nothing may be done, the BH army has the strength and the resources to move into those places within 48 hours. But what will happen to the left bank of Mostar? The industry in Vitez, especially the segments of the industry in Vitez that are important to this nascent state." Dr. Zuzul, did you know that towards the end of 1993, at the same time as negotiations were going on the BH army was moving to liberate, as they thought of it, Busovaca, Vitez, parts of Novi Travnik from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew about sporadic clashes and skirmishes in those areas, but I'm very surprised to see this transcript and to realise that those were planned operations. I had no inkling of that, and I believe no one on our side, none of those who participated in the negotiations, were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's see how the leadership in Sarajevo planned this offensive without having it become known. Pages 35, 36 in English. I will quote Stjepan Kljuic. "Can we do something for our own sake? Since you -- since we were accused at the United Nations. The finger was pointed at us. We have to respond. Why don't you appear on TV and say that the BH army is not mounting an offensive against Vitez, but between us, look, and I mean we're not children here. As Ivo says, someone has more life experience and more wisdom. Some speak more, some speak less and do more, et cetera. It is clear to all of us that strategically speaking, the most important for the BH army are Vitez and Novi Travnik because the industries are there, as my namesake said, that could carry us through another 20 years. And I said once, I said that to the president, for the sake of the international community you should say that we are not mounting any offensives, and second, strictly between us, by the 18th we should stop the offensive." Tell us, Dr. Zuzul, did you have any knowledge that Alija Izetbegovic or any of the representatives of the leadership in Sarajevo are making public statements that there was no offensive while a very fierce offensive was taking place on the ground and even the date of its termination was defined?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea, and I believe no one on our side in the negotiations had any idea. I'm happy that it eventually turned out that a solution can be found through negotiations, but I am sincerely astounded by this double play in politics, although I knew it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 4D 009300. It's a president's assertion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask a question which the answer seems implicitly to have been given by you, but still I think it's of some relevance. Do you know whether these discussions, and we're reading the text, the transcript of discussions, whether they led to any decision being taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to decisions in negotiations or decisions relative to the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm talking about decisions implemented some of the suggestion that are made in the discussion and that surprise you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot make any assertions because I do not know whether on the basis of this some actions followed, whether the decisions were indeed implemented by Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know that. However, by you leave, Your Honour, let me tell you why I said that I was astounded. If you remember, I personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. You have answered my question, actually, and I would not like this to lead to further time being consumed. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're aware that once a foundation is laid facts have to be proven about such policies, and this is something that the Defence will be doing in the following -- next months. The next document is 4D 00930. In other words, the document dated the 14th of January, 1993. Let's look at the page ending in numbers 232. In the English version this is page 9, and then 11 and the beginning of page 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: One participant at the meeting, Mr. Ljubjankic read a German report on the negotiations led in that period. Among other things, the BH army offensive against Vitez is mentioned. Let us focus on the statement by Alija Izetbegovic. I quote: "Because they said who would engage in the war effort now. I say we need Vitez for the sake of the future and not because we particularly wish to wage a war right now. We will be accused of wanting to capture Vitez in order to prolong the war. That's not why we're doing it. We need Vitez for the sake of our future." Tell us, Dr. Zuzul, did you have any knowledge that in early 1994 there had been fighting between the BH army and the HVO over Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific knowledge. I did, however, receive sporadic information about fighting in certain areas of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to one part of the German report Mr. Ljubjankic referred to. I quote: "In the last efforts to achieve peace it has become quite apparent that the Muslim army still treats the war option as option number one to say the least. Evidently they want to obtain from the Croats what it was impossible for them to obtain from the Serbs." Although there were other interesting remarks made here. Dr. Zuzul, tell us, in the course of international negotiations, was it your impression or did you have first-hand knowledge of the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo having realised that they did not stand a chance in the clashes against the army of Republika Srpska which was their superior and that they decided to try and gain what they could from the fighting against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I had any specific information to that effect. I can only say that this was the impression I had on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At page 240 onwards of the minutes, in English that's pages 19 and 20, Alija Izetbegovic again refers to that principle whereby unless everything is agreed nothing is agreed. Let us look at two of his sentences. I quote: "Of course we have to be in favour of an integral -- an integrated Bosnia-Herzegovina, but do not forget that the presence of that army is -- that that's the reason why we're contemplating a different solution other than that of an integrated state." Dr. Zuzul, did you have any knowledge about the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo realising that because of the Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska army could not achieve such an integrated state simply because the BH army did not have the strength to win that fight?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions so far I have said, and this is something the transcripts confirm now, that the objective of the Muslim leadership was to establish a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is impression that has been confirmed by actual events. The Muslim side was prepared to give up territory rather than to give up on the idea of a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina. Another impression of mine which is proved true by this transcript was that the Muslim side sometimes negotiated not in order to reach or find a solution but to play for time, which would allow them to create conditions conducive to a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me describe a situation I experienced. The talks were held, I believe, in Zagreb when President Tudjman told President Izetbegovic the following: "Alija, you say you have several hundred thousand dead. How many dead -- or how many more people should die before you should be prepared to negotiate a solution of sorts?" President Izetbegovic's response to that was, "Even if million -- a million of them died, a million would still be left to live their lives the way they should be lived." I'm quoting from memory here. This conversation remained deeply etched in my memory, in a way it does fit into the general picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zuzul, thank you very much. My cross-examination is finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I generously place the remainder of my time at the disposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Alaburic. You have been very generous indeed. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps -- perhaps it is important for the Bench to clarify what I think you do not misunderstand. Ms. Alaburic, of course, cannot dispose of her time in your favour, and you've got plenty anyway, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was said in jest. We know that we do have the same amount of time as the Prosecution but that that time cannot be given away in this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The jest was carried on, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Again, good afternoon and to counsel and to all of those in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Zuzul. Let me just say that much of your testimony so far has -- has gone a long way toward confirming much of the Prosecution case, so there will be many things that we won't, I think, need to talk about. I would like to ask you a number of questions about -- or some questions at least about your preparations. Before you came and appeared before the Chamber and gave your testimony in May, can you tell us a bit about what preparations you made in giving your testimony? Did you meet with anyone? Did you review documents? What steps did you take in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before that is answered, I don't want to be pedantic or difficult, but my learned friends for the Prosecution have on numerous occasions decried a proclivity of some members allegedly to insert comments in their questions, and in my respectful submission that is precisely what my learned friend Mr. Scott has done in his opening remarks about much of the Prosecution case being proved. That is a matter, of course, for Your Honours to decide in due course and I simply rise. I don't want silence in any way, shape, or form to be viewed as some kind of consent or acceptance or acquiescence of the statement put forward by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go ahead and tell us, please, about what preparations you made for giving you testimony starting in May, please.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, in order to prepare as best I could to help ascertain the truth and nothing but the truth - this is the way I see my evidence here - I met with the Defence for Mr. Prlic, reviewed the documents they placed at my disposal and went through these documents in my discussion with them. I had one telephone conversation with Madam Alaburic and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the course of meeting with the Defence for Mr. Prlic was any sort of a statement prepared or a summary or an outline of your testimony, anything that was prepared and put in front of you by way of review or something that would encapsulate or summarise, if you will, the testimony that you were expected to give?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since you -- you'll recall that when you left the courtroom room in May the President admonished you not to speak to anyone about your testimony between that time and today, and let me just inquire, have you talked with anyone about your testimony, either the testimony you've already gave or the testimony you anticipated starting or commencing again today? And by anyone, sir, I mean anyone. Have you spoken to anyone about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my wife was present at the time and is present here during my testimony. I wouldn't place her in any of the categories. Of course I discussed my evidence with her, and in very general terms I spoke with certain individuals who are part of my private life. But as I understood what the -- Their Honours said, I did not talk to anyone who would have been involved in this case in any way. I did not discuss the case with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, who were the certain individuals that you consider part of your private life that you spoke to about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very difficult to recall these individuals to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it's that difficult to recall, just how many people did you talk to about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the substance of my testimony. Well, I don't know. I don't think I talked about that to anyone. The fact remains that a good part of Croatia and a good part of Bosnia-Herzegovina know who I am and that I testified. This was published in the media. Everyone was able to follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I will have to sometimes, with my apology in advance, cut you off because I'm not interested about what was reported in the media. You said a few moments ago, you said, quote, and I'm looking at the transcript: "... certain individuals who were part of my private life." Now, please name some of those individuals, please.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Prosecutor. I fail to understand your question. I think you need to be more specific when you asked me what it is I talked about. Well, for instance, I spoke to my family about how I felt in the courtroom. Now, whether this comes into the category of discussing the testimony or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll put your family to one side, sir. Who else did you speak to about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't particularly recall who it was I spoke to. In my view, I did not speak with anyone about the substance of my testimony or the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since you appeared here in May anticipating at some point that you would be scheduled to come and complete your testimony, since you testified in May have you engaged in any other preparations, made any other reviews, reviewed any additional documents since beginning your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No specific documents. I apologise. Yes. I went through some documents published on the internet from some other cases. I read some books about that time period and territory, in particular this one book that is known to the Prosecution publish by the CIA analysts entitled "The Balkan Battlegrounds." This book helped refresh my memory of certain events. Other than that, I wouldn't say that I had any such activities, or I undertook any such activities with regard to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that you went through some documents published, excuse me, on the internet from some other cases, what other cases were they about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw part of the testimony of Mr. Mile Akmadzic on the internet. It was just a portion of it, not the entire testimony. And a part of Mr. Rebic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, what made you think that before coming back to give your testimony here under oath that you wanted to review Mr. Akmadzic's testimony and Mr. Rebic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, before answering the question I'm going to object to the line of questioning. There was no prohibition on any of that. Secondly, as I understand it and from my sources, the Prosecution has been very, very active in trying to dig up dirt onto this witness's private or past political affairs. So I don't think that there were any prohibitions. I don't think there's anything wrong with it. And in fact when the gentleman did ask for his -- a copy of his transcript, he was told that he could get it from the internet. So if we're going to put any limitations, then we should do that before the person leaves the courtroom, not at this point. And I object to this line of questioning. I would like to know what the relevance is, and I would like an answer and a ruling on my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution hasn't at this point suggested whether anything was improper or not but is simply inquiring so that the Chamber can fully assess the probative value and credibility of this witness, what he has done to prepare to testify, and if Mr. Karnavas doesn't have any objection to the content of it, that anyone can do this, then let's proceed with the questions. My question -- my pending question is: What made the witness think that he would want to review the testimony of Mr. Akmadzic and Mr. Rebic before resuming his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I did not use the term, and I believe I'm quite precise in my use of Croatian, and I speak English. I never said that I reviewed the testimonies of Mr. Akmadzic and Mr. Rebic. I simply said that since I was told that I could find transcripts of my own testimony on the internet and that -- that they could only be found on the internet, which is not the easiest way of looking through something, then I came across the transcripts of other testimonies, and it seemed only logical to go and see what the course of these testimonies was. Since the transcripts were quite long and I was away on holiday with my family, I only looked at them cursorily. As I've just said, nobody ever told me that this would be contrary to the rules binding me as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move forward to a few other basic points as we begin, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like for the witness to be shown in the Prosecution's book of maps, which is Exhibit P 09276, and whichever is easier, whether to put it on e-court or whether to give it to the witness in hard copy, but map number 1, the very first map in P 09276, or I'm told that there is a copy in binder 2, I'm told, if that also assists the courtroom. Are P 092 -- I'll make sure I get it right. P 09276. All right. Apparently we're having -- could we please have it on the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, if you can look on the screen in front of you, please, and I think this will be fully adequate for the present purposes. If you look at the map -- again for the record this is map number 1 in the Prosecution's book of maps, which is P 09276. And would you agree with me, sir, that in December 1990, following the elections, the first open elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were held in about November or December of 1990, every bit of the territory within these -- the bright red line surrounding what has been labelled as "Bosnia and Herzegovina," every bit of that territory belonged to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which at that time was completely within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be a precise map. In other words, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in December, if we go forward a year in time, if we go to December 1991, that remained exactly the same; correct? All the territory within that bright red line continued to be the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
