utterances.text: And moving forward to the end of May 1992, after Bosnia and Herzegovina had become an independent state and a Member State of the United Nations, these were -- this red line, this bright red line, these were the internationally recognised borders of that Member State of the United Nations and all the territory within that bright red line, without exception, was the sovereign territory of the UN Member State of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at least until mid-1994, at least, and every day in between, from May 1992 to the middle of 1994, every bit of that area remained the sovereign territory of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion that remained throughout a sovereign part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in a similar fashion, as of the time that Bosnia-Herzegovina became an independent state and a Member State of the United Nations, again in May 1992, from that time until at least mid-1994, the internationally recognised government of that UN Member State was the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was based, at least primarily, in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct in principle. I would not dare venture any assertions on where it was always stationed, where they was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the last part of your answer. It trailed off a bit, sir, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me try to explain. I believe that there had been moments where the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Presidency were unable to enter Sarajevo themselves, and to ask me to confirm that is too much, but in principle I believe what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I wasn't asking you any questions about freedom of movement or travel but simply can you confirm for us, this is a basic principle for the Judges, that nonetheless, whether you thought it was a good idea or a bad idea, whichever, the internationally recognised government of the UN Member State throughout this time period was the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, just one objection. I don't think it is in dispute that states are recognised by international law, not governments. Governments can change, but states always remain a subject to international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Be that as it may, Your Honour, that has no impact on my question whatsoever. My question to the witness, I believe he's answered it but given the additional qualification that he made, I just want the record to be very clear, the question is whether the internationally recognised government of that state was the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that at least primarily through this period was based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that time Sarajevo was the capital of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is not in dispute and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir. Was there any other government purported to represent the UN Member State of Bosnia and Herzegovina during that period of time that was recognised by the international community? Is there some other government out there somewhere that was representing this state?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Which period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Between as we said in my initial question, between May 1992, include up to mid-1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then I would object since we have had testimony that at various negotiations Izetbegovic was seen to be a representative of the Muslim nation, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let the Prosecutor do his work. We understand perfectly what the question is. We're waiting for the answer. Your objection is pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, because which -- because we have had testimony, we have had testimony where Mr. Akmadzic was there as the prime minister in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas, I do not quite understand the objections. Do you part from an assumption that every witness will say the same? If some witness has said something, do you think the same question cannot be put to the other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm looking at the question, Judge Trechsel, and we have had testimony that when there were international negotiations you had three different parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And that's it? That's the end of the matter? No other witness can be asked the same question, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have to assess the witness testimony that is given here, and we do not expect and cannot and should not expect every witness to say the same thing. If one witness had said something, another witness may say the same or may say something different, and I do not understand the justification of your objection, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if I could just get a ruling on my objection. My objection is I object to the form of the question as stated. It allows -- it has facts that are not -- that are not accurately portrayed in the evidence. My objection can be sustained or overruled and we'll move on, but I'm entitled to a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your objection is overruled. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, I'm not trying to -- I'm not trying to be difficult about this. I'm just trying to get a very clear answer. I'm not talking about who individual officials were or the fact that some of them may have worn different hats, and indeed the Chamber has heard about that. I'm talking about the government as an entity. The international community had to be dealing with someone. The United Nations sitting in New York had to deal with someone. It was a UN Member State. And that someone throughout this period time from May 1992 to the middle of 1994 was the government of that state, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm simply saying most people would refer to it sometimes as the Sarajevo government. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want real clarity, what you said is correct, but it's equally correct that the representatives who simultaneously represented Bosnia and Herzegovina appeared in negotiations about Bosnia and Herzegovina as representatives of one of the sides. To me that posed no problem. In my correspondent -- correspondence with Mr. Izetbegovic, I addressed him as president, president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although at one point it was quite unclear whether according to the constitution he indeed had that position. But to me it was indeed the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina except when they were acting as representatives of one of the sides in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You answered my question yes, sir. And in terms of other people that acted or wore different hats, you would agree in fact there were a number of people on the Croat side which also from time to time wore different hats, including one already mentioned, Mr. Akmadzic; correct? Sometimes he was acting on behalf of the HDZ. Sometimes he was acting on behalf of Herceg-Bosna. Sometimes he was the personal representative of Franjo Tudjman, and sometimes he was the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not confirm that because you have enumerated many hats, but, as I said earlier, it's not only true of Mr. Akmadzic. Mr. Izetbegovic himself sometimes acted as the president of SDA, a political party, sometimes as a representative of Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at other times as a president of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just in the same way that President Bush of the United States acts as the senior head of the Republican Party, and sometimes he acts as president of the United States. So I think we can establish that. Now, let's go forward to Greater Serbia. You used that concept at least seven or eight times in your direct testimony. You talked about Greater Serbia. Can you tell the Chamber what that means to you when you say Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true I used that term. I was not alone in that. I believe there was nearly a consensus among everyone whoever dealt with the history of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia that there existed in Serbia a group of intellectuals that promoted the concept of Greater Serbia, a Serbian state that would include all Serbs regardless of where they lived. And they even wrote that in so many words in the so-called memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Science, which is a public document. At one point in the early 1990s that policy began to be implemented with the occupation of certain territories in Croatia and later in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is how the plan of creating a Greater Serbia, so-called Greater Serbia, was being implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this follows from that, in fact, what you were just saying, but as part of that practice, and again in your testimony you used several times the phrase "ethnic cleansing," and I'd like for you to please tell the Judges what you mean when you use that term, what you understand that term to mean.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me and to most people that term means forcible expulsion of a certain part of a population from territories where they had lived for centuries only because they belonged to one ethnic community. And if I'm not mistaken that term was first used accurately in the case of the occupation of Vukovar when all the Croatian population, but not only, all non-Serb population was driven out from that area. And that repeated itself in other territories that were being occupied by Serbs and later in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, sir, when you use that term, and you talked about Vukovar and you can give me your next answer in reference to Vukovar if you wish or not, but you've mentioned forcible expulsion, and can you tell us what some other types of conduct or behaviour or practices do you understand to be part of ethnic cleansing or that took place as part of ethnic cleansing? And again, if you want to refer to Vukovar, please do.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spoken in very general terms, and although nothing good can be said of such ugly conduct, in addition to expulsions there were mass murders and mass deportations. I meant everything that led to a population to disappear from certain areas, and all of that did happen in Vukovar. Vukovar was the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you tell us what role does the destruction of religious or cultural or educational property, based on what you experienced and observed during these Balkan wars, what role does the destruction of cultural or religious or educational property play in ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the aggression, religious property was a particular target of destruction and that played a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why? What is it about destroying the others, and I use the term "the other," what is it about destroying the religious property associated with the other that is significant or a part of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer that question, because I wonder myself sometimes why, but if I try to think about it, not an acceptable but a rational reason would be to demonstrate to that population that they would never be able to come back to that area, because it's no secret that in those areas religious property is very important to preserving identity. It's also indisputable that some destruction occurred motivated purely by hatred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll come back to some of those topics again. I would like to turn now to just some of your positions that you've told us about. When you were an Assistant Foreign Minister, and I believe that was the first appointment that you received in the Croatian government, if I recall, when you were Assistant Foreign Minister, can you tell us who was your immediate superior; that is, who did you receive your tasks from, if you will? Who gave you directions? Who directed your work?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that brief period of about two months, Mr. Zvonimir Separovic was the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it that the answer then flows from that that he was the one who gave you your direction and tasks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did, and to some extent President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then when you were appointed Deputy Foreign Minister, the same question, sir, who was your superior at that point in the same sense that I just explained to you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Skrabalo was the minister, and with him I worked really as one team. We both reported to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then when you took on your position as UN representative -- excuse me, Croatia's representative to the UN in Geneva, who did you consider at that time to be your superior?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the Foreign Minister, Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that in formal terms only or was it actually Dr. Granic who actually supervised your work, gave you directions, what positions should be taken in Geneva, or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't just in formal terms. Mr. Granic was my superior, and we cooperated very well, but I received many instructions directly from President Tudjman, instructions as to how to act in negotiations. If you want to know more, in my normal daily work of a diplomat I communicated with the Foreign Ministry, with Mr. Granic as the minister and Mr. Sanader as Deputy Minister. In negotiations I communicated directly with President Tudjman even then, and especially when I became a special envoy of President Tudjman for these negotiations, and it was logical to talk directly with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just assist the Judges in having a bit more sense of your communications during that time period. Now we're talking about when you were a UN -- excuse me, the representative to the UN in Geneva. How often would you talk to, say, Mr. Granic or to President Tudjman? Is that something that would happen on a daily basis or once a week, or was there a regular morning telephone call? How would you -- how did you deal with these people?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I could say that I talked to Mr. Granic almost every day, a little less often with President Tudjman but still relatively often. During negotiations I would hear from him every day, but it was not a rule to report to him every day. It's just that I needed to keep him abreast of what was going on at the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me change to another individual, Mr. Susak. Had you known Mr. Susak before coming -- taking up your position first as assistant and then Deputy Foreign Minister?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I met him when I was in the Croatian army -- or, rather, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did you come to meet Mr. Susak at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was with a group of my colleagues, university professors, and we had this idea of creating a section for information and psychology work within the ministry, and that's when we met closer up with Minister Susak. I think we first spoke to General Tus and then with Minister Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you develop a relationship, though, with Mr. Susak after this initial acquaintance that you -- like with President Tudjman, Mr. Susak was someone that you had direct access to and would deal with directly?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relations with Minister Susak developed. We became friends almost. We communicated rather often, but it was not as often as I communicated with Minister Granic or President Tudjman. I don't remember a single case when Minister Susak had given me specific instructions on any score whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a small intervention in the translation. I said that I don't remember a single case when Minister Susak had given me, me as the ambassador, specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were an ambassador of Croatia to the UN in Geneva. The Prosecutor asked you how were the communications between Tudjman and Mr. Granic and yourself. You mentioned phone calls. You said how often those phone calls would take place, but I would like to know the following: As is the case in diplomatic matters often, do you send diplomatic telegrams, and would you receive specific instructions from Zagreb, or would everything take place over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In normal diplomatic work, in the operation of the mission at the United Nations in Geneva, I believe, our communication was similar to those of any other mission, through diplomatic channels: Telegrams, notes, et cetera. We sent them regularly, and we received them regularly, including instructions. Because in a way, ever since I had left for Geneva, I had a dual role. One was to do the regular diplomatic work at the mission with the United Nations, and we performed this in the same way as every other mission did. As far as monitoring the conference on the former Yugoslavia was concerned and participating in negotiations, most of the communication went again through standard diplomatic channels. However, oftentimes communication was direct, by telephone, because quite simply things were happening too fast, and I had both the instructions and the right to make the judgement myself when something was urgent enough to contact directly the minister or the head of state without going through the usual diplomatic channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, I'd like to turn next please to Mate Boban, who you mentioned in your testimony before. You said you had known Mr. Boban before, that in fact you grew up in the town, Imotski, where Mr. Boban worked, and as part of your testimony you said that just before the developments that you had just been discussing and that you had just been discussing December of 1991 you said: "I had been directly in touch with Mr. Boban." Do you have any recollection of what business you had with Mr. Boban in approximately December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly what I said, I said I was indirectly in contact with Mr. Boban, and that's because my friend and his cousin, I suppose, Mr. Marinko Boban, contacted Mr. Mato Boban regarding possible organising of volunteers to assist with the liberation of Dubrovnik, and I don't recall any direct talk with him, with Mr. Boban, in December 1991. No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't intend to spend much time on that given everything we need to talk about. You did -- it was transcribed at page 26789 to 90 that you had "I had been directly in touch with Mr. Boban during that time," but I take it now that's been corrected. What kind of relationship following that time did you develop with Mr. Boban in these -- in the years 1992, 1993, 1994, since he was the president of Herceg-Bosna, which I think we can all agree was something that impacted your life at that time a fair amount. What was the nature of your dealings with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't quite understood your statement, Mr. Prosecutor, but as I understand it, I cannot agree at all that my acquaintance with Mr. Mate Boban had significant bearing on my life. It had no significant bearing on my life whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I said was in reference to Herceg-Bosna, which I think that we can agree did have, at least as a topic, as something that was going on at the time, did have a substantial bearing on your life or probably you wouldn't be here. So in that regard, in regard to your dealings with Herceg-Bosna or touching on Herceg-Bosna, can you tell the Judges, please, what relationship did you develop with Mate Boban during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Prosecutor, I will start by telling you that not even Herceg-Bosnia had a significant bearing on my life. The Republic of Croatia did and my work for the Republic of Croatia, but not Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, be that as it may, sir, and we'll have a lot of time to talk about these specific topics, but tell us about your relationship with Mr. Boban during that time.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we knew each other in private life. We would be in touch whenever he came to Geneva. He would come to visit our mission as well. Sometimes, not always, I accompanied him to various meetings. On occasion we discussed political issues. Sometimes I expressed my disagreement with some of his thoughts or actions. At any rate, I received instructions from Zagreb and behaved the way I was told to behave by my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you about some of the things you've disagreed with. You said, "Sometimes I expressed my disagreement with some of his thoughts or actions." Can you identify some of those thoughts or actions that you disagreed with?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My style is markedly different from that of Boban. His tough approach did not always help resolve matters, and my remarks were along those lines. I regularly told President Tudjman and the minister what the situation was like with regard to negotiations, and I left the decision up to them, whether they felt that they need to intervene either toward Mr. Boban or toward anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you disagreed with his style. Did you disagree with any of his policies or behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Prosecutor, I was an ambassador, and I tried to professionally perform my role. I was not a politician in Geneva. I did not deal with politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Let me just ask you as a human being at the moment. Let's put aside being an ambassador. Did you ever disagree with any -- the substance or policies espoused by Mr. Boban during this time in any capacity, private, personal, official, whatever? You said you disagreed with him in style. Did you disagree with any of his behaviour, actions, or policies?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to answer that question in general terms. If you ask me about a specific situation I can give you my opinion, but where can you find a situation where everyone agrees with everyone especially whens such complex issues are at stake. Of course I did not agree with many politicians and many individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... something important. I'm sure you won't use the Judges's time to talk about something trivial. So please talk about something important. Please talk about some important disagreement you had with Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that you should put that question to me in reference to a specific situation. I'm giving you a general answer to a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you go please -- can I please direct your attention to exhibit -- excuse me. Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit P 10402. It should be in one of your binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be, Your Honours, in binder number 2. No, excuse me. My apology. Binder number 3. P 10402. And if I can have that on --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, to turn particularly to -- and you can look at either one that assist you the most, the English or Croatian language. These are excerpts from the book by Mate Granic, and in particular on page 70 of his book, or in the excerpts you'll just see on page 5 of the English version you'll see a reference to page 70. Mr. Granic says in his book: "Mate Boban had a special role in this conflict. I had heard of him for the first time in 1992 when he became the leader of the HDZ in BH. We were formally introduced soon afterwards but our first serious dealings only after I became -- had," excuse me, "but had our first serious dealings only after I had become head of Croatian diplomacy. We attended several meetings between the Croatian authorities and Croats in BH. We were never close, and we supported completely different positions. Boban was a very narrow-minded man, full of hatred for the Bosniaks. He supported Bosnian Serbs, believing that he could enter into an agreement with them regardless of the criminal policies of Karadzic, Mladic, and their assistants. It was clear to me that he was the biggest obstacle to peace in BH. At meetings he never spoke about the Bosniaks or Muslims but only used words like Turks or Balija." Now, how does Mr. Granic's description of Mr. Boban fit with your experience? Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Granic's opinion which he wrote a number of years later. He did not express his opinion in these terms in the period of time we're discussing. Still, I can agree with some aspects of what he said here. I was under the impression that Mr. Boban felt that he could find a common language with the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina more easily than with the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Regardless of that, I would not say that Mr. Boban was the biggest obstacle to peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how about --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's taking it a bit too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how about the statements that he was full of hatred for the Bosniaks and he always spoke about them using terms like Turks or Balija. Was that your experience dealing with him?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear him use these terms, but I would definitely not say that he used these terms all the time. He sometimes referred to them as Muslims and sometimes as Turks or Balija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just hopefully finish with this because I think we may be coming up on the time for the break, but in the middle of that paragraph Dr. Granic says: "We supported completely different positions." Now, you worked closely on these issues for some period of years. You worked closely, as you've told us already, with Dr. Granic. Can you tell us how Dr. Granic's positions differed from Mr. Boban's positions, because Dr. Granic says they were completely different.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He makes a general statement here which refers to a large period of time. In my view, at some point there was a great difference in principled views between Mr. Granic and me on the one hand and Mr. Boban and others on the other, and this preceded the Washington -- that was about the Washington agreements -- or, rather, about the possibility of establishing a federation of Croats and Muslims. Both Dr. Granic and I thought that this was a possible and implementable option. And as can be gleaned from the transcripts, this opinion was shared by President Tudjman too. In my view, Mr. Boban did not believe this viable. That was the biggest difference in opinion at the time, and I think that this is what Dr. Granic referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Chamber will bear with me for one moment just so we can finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Boban did not believe this viable, I want you to be very clear. When you refer to "this," what was it that Mr. Boban did not believe viable?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I spoke quite extensively of the fact that at some point in time during the negotiations, in particular with American representatives but also with representatives of the Muslims, we started working on the agreement about setting up the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did Mr. Boban not find viable? Not about what the Americans said or what the Muslims said. What did Mr. Boban not find viable?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this was precisely what I was about to tell you. Mr. Boban thought that such a federation could not be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to try the Chamber's patience. We can come back to it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A mistake in the transcript. Page 56, line 18, in the English transcript we can read Judge Antonetti, whereas it was the witness speaking at this point. We're going to break for 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, in the interest of time I'm going to try and move forward to some other topics. It's fair to say, is it not, that from 1990 and until such time as their status as independent states was internationally recognised, both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were part of the state of Yugoslavia, the territory of which extended to the external borders, if you will, of the various republics of the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that they were part of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia until their independence was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And up until the time that their independence was declared and recognised, the armed forces of that internationally recognised state, that is, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the armed forces of that state could be garrisoned and moved about within the borders of that state; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as they constituted the armed forces of that state and for as long as that state existed, yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that in general in those respects both President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic, in 1990 and 1991, faced a very similar situation in reference to the state that they were part of and to the military forces of that state; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At least during 1990 and well into 1991, neither Mr. -- neither country, I shouldn't just refer to them as individuals, Mr. Tudjman or Mr. Izetbegovic, but neither Croatia nor the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had any substantial military force separate from or not controlled by, ultimately, the Yugoslavia federal government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until one point both the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including all the other republics of the former Yugoslavia had the Territorial Defence, which was under the control of the republican, not federal institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in approximately 1990, is it correct that both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina the JNA, by one means or another, seized the weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence in both of those republics? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you testified, in fact, that then when the armed conflict with the JNA or the forces of the former Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia, perhaps, when that conflict broke out, Croatians -- Croatia's military abilities were actually quite limited. You actually said at one point they were "pitifully weak," and they were not able to defend Croatia against the JNA forces in substantial parts of the territory of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, and if you remember from being a citizen and living in that country at the time, that there was a fair amount of criticism directed at President Tudjman that he had not -- he and his government had not done more to prepare for military conflict with Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such criticism, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, and just -- and you did touch upon this in your testimony before that by approximately the second half of 1991, Serb forces of the JNA occupied as much as -- or at least one-third of Croatia's territory?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's, roughly speaking, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated during your direct examination that during this time that the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not do anything to protest the JNA actions or to support Croatia in connection with these various events in 1990 and 1991, and I want to direct your attention particularly there came a time, I believe, sir, on the 9th of January, 1991, where the Yugoslav -- federal Yugoslav Presidency or government ordered illegal paramilitary forces in the republics to disarm. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do recall stating in my testimony that the general impression was that the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina was doing nothing to support Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that on the 21st of January, 1991, the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina backed and supported both Slovenia and Croatia in their conflict with the Yugoslav Presidency and urged the Yugoslav Presidency to reconsider its actions in threatening to disarm alleged paramilitary forces in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but I do not exclude that it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall that in August 1991, both Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia announced that they would not allow their conscripts to perform national service outside their republics?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do recall that vaguely. I don't recall exactly when and how it was formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that brings us up to this so-called statement by Mr. Izetbegovic, "It's not our war," and you talked about that in your testimony at page 27618. Now, the Chamber has heard quite a bit of evidence about that. Mr. Izetbegovic made that statement on the 6th of October, 1991, and I wonder, did you hear Mr. Izetbegovic make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not personally present when the statement was made, but there were so many reports of it that I believed at the time, and I still do believe that he stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, that particular four words, if you will, "It's not our war," was part of a much more extensive statement that he made at the time. I'm wondering if you ever actually read the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, do you remember the context in which Mr. Izetbegovic said that, "It's not our war"? In the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the statement, but I do remember the context of the events in Croatia and the territory in general. This statement received quite a great deal of coverage in the media in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you've told us, sir, that you didn't hear him make that statement, and you don't recall ever reading the full statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it fair to say that that is something that you've repeated, like so many others, taking Mr. Izetbegovic's words out of context, having no knowledge of the statement in which -- the context of the statement in which they were made?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. I believe that I'm pretty well familiar with the context of political events and what the impact of such a statement amid such events was at the time when Yugoslavia was breaking up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can't tell us, sir, what the rest of the statement was. Do you recall around that same time on the 20th of September, 1991, Stipe Mesic, who at that time was serving as the Yugoslav president, called on JNA soldiers to desert and go over to the side of the elected leadership in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that vaguely. I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, wasn't President Izetbegovic's statement a few days later an expression of solidarity with Stipe Mesic and Croatia when Izetbegovic says, "It's not our war," calling for Bosnia's young men, its conscripts, it's young men, not to go and fight in the JNA war against Croatia? That's what his statement said if you've ever cared to read the entire statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. This is testimony now from counsel, and I'm rather surprised that the Bench is not reacting a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All of which is based on the evidence in the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may be heard for my objection and then the gentleman can say whatever he wishes. If we trace the previous questions and answers, the witness has indicated that he hasn't seen it. He vaguely recalls, and so on. Now a question is put, and then afterwards there is a declarative statement made by the Prosecution, no inflection. In fact, it is testimony. I object to that. In believe Mr. Khan quite eloquently informed us about the evils of such statements. I would respect the rules, and I would ask that the Prosecutor be cautioned, just as I'm cautioned on occasion when I get carried away. I would ask the same thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I think you're quite right. Mr. Scott, why don't you put the documents to the witness? You have other ways of bringing him to where you want to bring him, and I think counsel's objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness is he has not seen or read the statement, so I'll leave it at that rather than showing him a statement that he's never seen before, but the Chamber has.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, around this same time period in 27 of January, 1991, you recall President Tudjman endorsing the JNA's right to arrest individuals who at the time were mainly activists of Croatia's ruling party concerning the illegal possession of arms. Do you recall Mr. Tudjman endorsing the JNA's right to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that I never saw Mr. Izetbegovic's statement. I saw the statement on several occasions. I just said that I didn't hear it. Those are two different things. Secondly, what you've just said is something I sincerely don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, since you come back to it, I'll just ask you again. Tell us what the rest of the statement -- what the rest of Mr. Izetbegovic's statement says. You say you've seen it several times. Tell us, please, apart from those four words that you remember, what was the context? What was said above those four words? What was said after those four words, and tell us what the context and import of that statement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think we need to be fair to the witness, after all of these years to ask the witness to recall something that was said years and years ago. I believe Judge Trechsel indicated the method by which this sort of technique should be used. I did -- I did not give any hints to the Prosecution because I'm not here to tell him how to do his job, but I think that's the proper way. He can show him, and then if wants to further cross-examine him on that and confront him then that's fine, but I think it's rather unfair to ask a witness to recall something that he heard 15 years ago. Let's be realistic here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know what you want to highlight so I'll let you ask your questions, but as was pointed out by Mr. Karnavas it would be saving time if you had the exact statement in the context of Mr. Izetbegovic. You may as well show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't have time, Your Honour, to do that. And the point's already been made. The point has already been made. I don't know want to argue with him about what I show him in the document. The point is he doesn't remember anything about it except "It's not our war," and that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall that in May 1991 President Tudjman supported a unanimous decision by the collective federal Yugoslav Presidency to grant the JNA more authority to deal with ethnic conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truly I don't remember. I was in the United States of America at the time. The information you're asking me about is too specific. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall this situation where in May of 1991 President Tudjman urged a group of ethnic Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Mostar area, who had been protesting, carrying on a two-day blockade of a JNA convoy, that they should stop their protest and let the JNA proceed on its way? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm going to object to this technique. Either show the documents and confront the witness, but to ask the witness to remember things or to recall is virtually impossible at this stage. Now, I don't object to this form of questioning. However, if this is going to be the basis upon which later there's going to be a motion to introduce documents, I will high object because now we're not giving the witness an opportunity to look at the documents. What is the basis for Mr. Scott's pronouncements? I don't know. I think we're entitled to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. You're asking him whether he recalls, and he said he couldn't remember because at the time he was in the United States of America. Very well. Then to refresh his memory you should show him in the document. You should say here is the document showing this and he can say whether he's seen it or not, whether he was in the USA and he had other things to do other than watch documents -- or read documents and watch the media.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was do you recall Mr. Tudjman urging ethnic Croats near Mostar to stop blockading the JNA blockade in about May 1991? You either remember or you don't. If you don't remember, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already said that I didn't remember specific events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you remember in October 1991 and following the Tudjman government allowing JNA forces to leave their barracks in Croatia and take with them their weapons, their tanks, and their ammunitions when they left?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it did in part. Of course the motivation of President Tudjman was that the Yugoslav People's Army should leave Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And they were allowed to leave with their weapons, tanks, and ammunition in hand; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the details. I think it's quite difficult to give a general answer, because if I'm -- unless I'm mistaken, the situation was different in different parts of Croatia. In some areas commanders of the Yugoslav army units simply laid down their weapons, in others they tried to resist. So it's very difficult to give a general answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the point of this is that isn't it not correct that in 1990 and 1991 the ability of either Mr. Izetbegovic or Mr. Tudjman to do much of anything to stop the JNA was very, very limited? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was limited, but time showed that it was not impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Time showed. You said at one point that Mr. Izetbegovic believed at the time, and I believe this was when you were referring to this you were talking about June 1991, that the JNA, the federal Yugoslav forces would not attack Bosnia and Herzegovina. You gave that testimony at page 27687 of the transcript. And my question to you again, sir, during much of 1990 and 1991, hadn't that exactly also been President Tudjman's position or belief, that he could avoid an armed conflict or war with Yugoslavia and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a certain period of time in 1990 I do believe that this was a position of President Tudjman. In other words, that through negotiations and an intervention from the international community a solution could be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And indeed wasn't that, however, the exact point of the meetings between Tudjman and Milosevic in Karadjordjevo, to negotiate a deal by which Croatia would not be attacked and the two of them would turn their attention instead on Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what was discussed at Karadjordjevo, because nobody was there except Tudjman and Milosevic. So nobody knows directly what they talked about. Having met Mr. Tudjman later, I know for a fact that his motive for going to meet Milosevic was to try to stop the war and to try to find a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we -- we won't stop to pull the map out. If anyone questions it I'm sure I'll be corrected, but if you look at a map of the former Yugoslavia, sir, you will see that Serbia has no contiguous border with Slovenia, and yet it's correct, was it not, that the JNA was also attacking and resisting the independence declared by Slovenia at that time? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know anything that President Tudjman or the Tudjman government did to prevent the JNA from crossing Croatia territory to carry out these actions in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I can see what logic you are guided by, I have to say that everybody who knew the situation realised quite clearly that Croatia was not able to stop the Yugoslav People's Army. And in any case, this intervention by the JNA lasted only ten days. Slovenia did not start any serious war, nor was Croatia in any position to help Slovenia, nor had the JNA, as we can see from numerous documents, any serious intentions. Slovenia and Croatia, nevertheless, had identical political positions and assisted each other in many ways. There is an imprecision in interpretation. I said "fully," not "in many ways."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether President Tudjman ever told Kadijevic that Croatia would not meddle in Serbia's dispute with Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've also talked about, in this -- in fact, in these same set of facts, essentially, that the people in both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina took steps to essentially arm themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that people armed themselves both in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you agree, sir, that the Muslim side had every much right to prepare for a conflict and arm themselves as the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there might be something unclear in your answer. Maybe it was due to the question. The arming of the population, was it spontaneous, or did someone tell them to arm themselves, because that would not be the same situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. President. I would have answered precisely, but I had not understood the question very precisely. I'm not -- I think there were two parallel things going on in Croatia. People organised themselves spontaneously. I witnessed that myself. A large majority of my colleagues tried to get hold of a weapon without any specific purpose in mind, but on the other hand, the government was also trying in various ways to get hold of armaments and to assure its defence. So there were two processes going on in parallel, and there was a third process as well. A large number of Croats who had emigrated tried to assist by sending weapons, I believe both to Croatia and to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me correct myself, not only Croats but others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this additional answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate the clarification. I should have been clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to stay on that for one moment longer, sir. Is it fair to say that in that situation that we've been discussing, both the Croatian government and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina as governments were taking steps to organise themselves, to arm themselves, and various individuals and groups were also engaged in such efforts? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the topic of some of the peace negotiations that you were involved in, and we've talked a fair amount today in connection with the questions by Ms. Alaburic about the process of negotiations, and you had indicated in your direct examination, sir, that negotiations normally result in some sort of compromise; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And each side or party to a negotiation, broadly speaking, is entitled to their positions, and they can drive a hard bargain; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm sure in your experience there's a number of different negotiating tactics and methods, and people use different methods and different approaches to try to get what they want; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as frustrating as that process may be, it may be very aggravating, in fact, but that's the negotiating process; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You talked about situations where representatives of the Muslim party might come and receive information but not be in a position to make a decision. Now, I put to you, sir, I suspect that's not uncommon in your experience. A party may come to a meeting and say, "We're here to listen. We'd like to hear what you have to say. We're not in a position to make any decision today, but please lay out your position to us." There's nothing particularly uncommon about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't, but if you use that strategy to obstruct negotiations, then we cannot talk of it as something positive. I've never claimed that that's the way they used this strategy. I just shared my impression that occasionally that is the way they were trying to negotiate without actually agreeing to anything. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you -- could you agree that the opposite, if you've said that -- if I can paraphrase and I'll try to get it correctly, that, one, this idea that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, but would you agree that the opposite can be equally destructive or misleading or non-productive and that is, the position that as soon as one thing is agreed, acting as if everything has been agreed?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly. Every method, every approach used to obstruct negotiations is equally negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just be very transparent with you, sir. The position of many, and the Chamber has heard some of the witnesses in this courtroom, is that the problem encountered on the Croat side, as it were, I'm not talking about you personally, sir, generally speaking, was that when something -- when one part of something would be agreed, the Croat side would then immediately act as if everything had been agreed and that they were ready to move forward on everything whether there was, in fact, agreement or not. Have you ever heard that commentary made?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any specific example, but it is true that the Croat side was keen to go forward with the implementation as soon as something was agreed, guided simply by the idea that the sooner something is implemented, if it had been agreed already, the sooner the objectives will be reached, namely, to stop the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say, sir, that on a number of occasions, both the international negotiators and/or the Serbs and/or the Muslim party on a number of occasions would say, "Hold on. We're not there yet. Yes, we've agreed to something, some parts but not everything, and we're not ready to go forward further"? Didn't that happen on a number of occasions? January 1993, March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. Certainly such things happened in all sorts of negotiations, especially the very complex ones like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In one of your -- in some of your earlier testimony you were talking about one of the meetings -- one of the presidential meetings in June 1991, and there were negotiations involving -- well, the positions of Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Gligorov at one point, and Tudjman was quoted as saying, and again this is in the transcript of the 8 June 1991 meeting, P 00037, and Tudjman is quoted as saying, "Basically, that is, Serbia accepted it but giving it its own interpretation." Now, what does that mean to you? You say a party has accepted the position, but giving it its own interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not interpret this sentence because I don't know in which context it belongs, when it was said and what it applies to, but generally speaking we all know of examples when one side says they had accepted something and then interprets it as something entirely different. I doubt that I have ever quoted Tudjman off-the-cuff like this. Now, this sentence, when I see it like this in English, I can't place it in what I might have said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I don't want you to feel misled. This was a statement attributed to President Tudjman in the presidential transcript. I was just putting it to you for your comment as an experienced negotiator. When someone says one party has accepted a position but given it its own interpretation, and I think you addressed that, but I wasn't attributing the statement to you, sir. Now, you've talked about the Washington Agreement, and you told us that you became involved in that process very early on and that you were involved, in fact, in some of the preliminary steps, if you will, to initiate that process; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you recall approximately when the Washington process started as opposed to any of the previous efforts? We are not talking about Owen-Stoltenberg. We're not talking about anything -- but when something began to be called Washington, when did that process start?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact dates. I'm sure they're easy to find. But speaking of the situation at the negotiations, I believe two important factors determined the beginning of the Washington process. First was the direct involvement of the US, that is, sending Mr. Redman as a special envoy of President Clinton, and second was the feeling that prevailed in everyone. I believe that the peace conference, the way it ran in Geneva, had reached a dead end. I believe those were two important elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, sir, that both in your prior testimony and in some of the presidential meetings where you were a participant you confirmed that and which hopefully we need not spend more time on that. It's fair to say that by the latter part of 1993, all of the previous peace processes were basically dead, so to speak; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the prevailing impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think at one point in one of your statements you said that the conference, the ICFY, was -- essentially had run its course and was no longer productive. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you talked about some of the things leading up to Washington or the fact that the -- this -- one of the important aspects, the direct and increasing involvement of the United States government, but let me also ask you this: Is it fair to say that by late 1993, early 1994, the Bosnian Croats in particular were under tremendous military pressure in Bosnia and Herzegovina - the war had essentially turned against them at that point - and Croatia was under tremendous international pressure because of certain concerns about its involved in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Aren't those two things true?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not comment on the situation in the conflict on the ground. There are certainly other people who know that better. But it's true that Croatia was under a certain pressure from the international community at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as things headed in the direction of Washington but even before it was formally known as Washington, you had expressed a view, had you not, that a -- some sort of a unification between the Croats and Muslims alone in the same entity, that that was not -- to use Mr. Boban's word, that was not viable. That had been your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn, please, in your binder to -- I'll tell you which binder in a moment, Exhibit P 10532 should be in the third binder. P 10532. Sir, this is a press account by the BBC on the 9th of August, 1993, in connection with ongoing negotiations at the time. You were interviewed, described here as the head of Croatian mission to the UN in Geneva, and in the last part of that -- in the last paragraph that of that article you say: "Asked why the Muslim idea of unification of Muslim and Croat republics into a Bosnia-Herzegovina union is not acceptable, Zuzul said, 'It could hardly work.'" Why did you think a unification of Muslims and Croats in a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina "could hardly work"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really recall that statement, although I have no reason to claim it's not true. But if I had said that, then I must have believed at that moment that it couldn't work. Still, I continued or started to work actively for that solution in which it could work. So if I had said that, it applied only to that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said earlier today, I believe, that -- you talked -- made reference to the fact that maps had been prepared by the international representatives involved, but just to be clear here, because in the previous paragraph you're commenting on the allocation of territory. The Bosnian Muslims would get 30 per cent, et cetera. I mean, isn't it fair to say, sir, that all the parties were constantly preparing and submitting maps throughout this process?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's completely correct, but I was talking about the map that was part of the Vance-Owen Plan, because I think that was the question. The map was shown to me, and I believe I said it had been prepared by international experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, moving on Washington, that -- further into it, if you will, that as it ultimately came about and as ultimately signed by the Croat and Muslim parties, that the Washington Agreement was a fairly radical shift from the previous peace plans and represented a substantial turn in Croatia's position or policy?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say whether it represented a turn, because even before there had been talk about a federation and a confederation between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, I believe it represented a concrete and realistic possibility of reaching an agreement which at that moment was being supported by the majority of important international factors -- players.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, please, to go to -- we won't be able to finish this tonight, but I suppose we should use the time. If you can go to Exhibit P 07856, which should be in binder number 2. 7856. Sir, this is -- as you're looking there for the record, let me say this is a record of a meeting with President Tudjman and others in Zagreb on the 13th of February, 1994. You can refer to -- there should be both in English and a Croatian language transcript there, and you can refer to whichever is most convenient for you. Looking at page number 1, and the page numbers should be the same in both versions, President Tudjman, if you will, calls this meeting to order, and he says: "Gentlemen, I told Minister Susak to invite Mate and the rest of you - a summit of the leading people of Herceg-Bosna - for us to come to an agreement as to how and what to take forward after all that has happened recently: Our general meeting in Livno, the Sarajevo meeting, the current talks in Geneva, but above all regarding the new situation arising from the initiative taken by the United States with a group of European countries for an ongoing solution to the Bosnia-Herzegovina crisis." Now, the new situation, sir, that's referred to by President Tudjman here, that's Washington; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the beginning, which leads towards the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can continue over to page number 2, skipping to the last paragraph on that page. President Tudjman continues talking and says: "At the same time, pressure on us publicising," apparently some omission, something that's been left out. "So far they have let it be known that they are not happy with our policy in Herceg-Bosna, that we are to blame for worsening relations with the Muslims, and they have let us know that we must change this and quite openly make Mate Boban a symbol of this supposed responsibility of ours for the clash with the Muslims. It was said then in friendly talks that we must change this symbol, which is why I decided that Mate would take no more part in the talks ..." Do you recall -- do you recall the decision being made by President Tudjman that Boban would no longer participate in the negotiations in early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Mate Boban stopped participating in the negotiations at that time and that President Tudjman wanted him to stop, but whether anyone made a formal decision about that and who made it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to page 4 of the record. President Tudjman refers to the ongoing discussions, and about a third of the way down that page it says: "We are for a union of three republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the question could be raised and Ambassador Zuzul, who spoke to the American envoy Redman, who was in charge of it, will tell you we could find ourselves in a delicate position if that American and Western policy were to go as far as allowing the departure of the Serbs ..." Now, on the Croat side, and I don't mean the Bosnian Croats but in terms of the Croats from the Republic of Croatia, were you leading the negotiations around that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not leading the negotiations, but I participated in them. Now, in this specific case I believe I reported to the president about talks with Ambassador Redman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the top of page 5, Tudjman continues and he says and about this process: "At the same time as we find ways and means to come to an agreement with the Muslims, but an agreement which will not bring in question our interest in Herceg-Bosna or our state interest as a whole." Now, this record will show, sir, and we probably won't get to it tonight, but that you were present in this meeting. What did you understand President Tudjman to mean when he says, "We will not allow the agreement to put in question our interest in Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then and now my interpretation was that he meant protection of the constitutive status of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's as far as we can go this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, some recommendations on my part since you are to return tomorrow. The hearing will start at 9.00 in the morning. You're not supposed to have any contact whatsoever, but for the members of your family, of course, you are free to convey your impressions about the hearing to them as long as it doesn't go beyond the family circle. You're also free to read any book that is available to you. We are not here to exert censorship and we are not to prohibit any reading which might seem useful to you. This is what I wanted to tell you. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
